title: Words at War 43-06-24 (01) Combined Operations (1943-06-24)
plotSynopsis: An imaginative reconstruction based on Combined Operations follows a British soldier who volunteers for commando service, survives punishing training and joins a raid on the German-held French coast. The raiders demolish military installations while suffering heavy losses, and a delayed explosive charge aboard the HMS Campbeltown later destroys the dock area and kills German personnel examining the ship. The narrator frames the raid as preparation for the larger assault on Hitler's occupied Europe and as a tribute to the men who died gaining that experience.

title: Words at War 43-07-10 (03) They Call It Pacific (1943-07-10)
plotSynopsis: A dramatized selection from correspondent Clark Lee's They Call It Pacific traces the collapse of early Allied confidence as Japan sweeps through the Pacific. Lee moves from Shanghai to Manila, watches the destruction following Pearl Harbor, reports from the Philippines and Bataan, and records the belief that American reinforcements will arrive even as the military position deteriorates. He eventually escapes toward Australia while friends and fellow correspondents are killed. The program ends with Lee imagining the eventual return to the Philippines, China and Tokyo, framing his experiences as lessons learned at enormous cost.

title: Words at War 43-07-17 (04) the Last Days of Sevastopol (1943-07-17)
sortKey: 0|1943-07-17|00004|words at war 43-07-17 (04) the last days of sevastopol (1943-07-17)
plotSynopsis: A dramatization of Boris Voyetekhov's The Last Days of Sevastopol follows a Soviet correspondent into the besieged city during its final defense against German forces. He witnesses ruined streets, wounded civilians, children involved in reconnaissance, exhausted troops and artillery crews continuing to fight under relentless air and ground attack. The program culminates in the desperate battles of late June and July 1942, portraying Sevastopol's defenders as continuing their resistance even as the city is reduced to rubble and defeat becomes unavoidable.

title: Words at War 43-07-24 (05) the Ship (1943-07-24)
plotSynopsis: The British light cruiser HMS Artemis escorts a vital convoy through the Mediterranean while enemy aircraft, cruisers and battleships close in. Officers and ratings at every station struggle to keep the ship fighting as damage mounts and the captain balances protecting the convoy against the temptation to chase the enemy. Torpedoes, gunfire and disciplined damage control finally force the opposing force to turn away, allowing the convoy to continue. As darkness falls, the captain reflects that winning the battle is only part of the larger struggle and that preserving freedom will demand vigilance and purpose long after the shooting ends.

title: Words at War 43-07-31 (06) from the Land of Silent People (1943-07-31)
sortKey: 0|1943-07-31|00006|words at war 43-07-31 (06) from the land of silent people (1943-07-31)
plotSynopsis: A dramatized eyewitness report from Robert St. John's From the Land of Silent People recounts scenes from Yugoslavia and Greece as Axis occupation and war overwhelm civilian life. St. John's narrator describes bombings, refugees, military retreat, shortages and encounters with ordinary people trying to survive, including the recurring figure of Sonia. The program is structured as reportage rather than a single plot and closes with St. John reflecting on the occupied peoples who have been forced into silence but continue resistance while waiting for Allied liberation.

title: Words at War 43-08-07 (07) Prisoner of the Japs (1943-08-07)
plotSynopsis: American correspondent Gwen Dew is trapped in Hong Kong when Japan attacks in December 1941. She lives through the siege, surrender and months of internment marked by hunger, brutality and humiliation, while continuing to observe her captors as a reporter. Colonel Tada even summons her for an interview in which he boasts about Japan's ambitions. After seven months, Dew is included in a civilian prisoner exchange and sails toward freedom, ending her account by reminding listeners that many Allied prisoners remain behind.

title: Words at War 43-08-14 (08) Love at First Flight (1943-08-14)
plotSynopsis: A comic adaptation of Love at First Flight follows Lester Dowd from his post-Pearl Harbor decision to join the Navy through the absurdities of aviation training. Medical exams, drills, airsickness, romantic letters and repeated misunderstandings turn his pursuit of wings into a string of comic mishaps, including an embarrassing incident in which he cannot unlock his aircraft brakes. By graduation he has become a naval aviator, while the woman he hoped to marry has married someone else, leaving Dowd to laugh at the final irony.

title: Words at War 43-08-19 (09) Last Days of Sevastopol (1943-08-19)
sortKey: 0|1943-08-19|00009|words at war 43-08-19 (09) last days of sevastopol (1943-08-19)
plotSynopsis: A repeat broadcast of the dramatization of Boris Voyetekhov's The Last Days of Sevastopol follows a Soviet correspondent through the besieged city during its final defense against German forces. He encounters ruined neighborhoods, wounded civilians, young reconnaissance helpers, mine layers and exhausted artillery crews continuing to fight under relentless attack. The recording culminates in the battles of late June and July 1942 as Sevastopol is reduced to rubble, preserving the defenders' endurance even as defeat becomes unavoidable.

title: Words at War 43-08-21 (10) Malta Spitfire (1943-08-21)
plotSynopsis: A dramatization of George F. Beurling and Leslie Roberts' Malta Spitfire traces Beurling from a Canadian boy obsessed with airplanes to a fighter pilot defending Malta. Rejected at first because he lacked the expected schooling, he persists until he reaches combat, where experience teaches the fiercely independent flyer that survival depends on teamwork as well as marksmanship. During the siege of Malta he helps defend vital convoys against Axis aircraft, is eventually shot down and badly wounded, and is presented as one of the young pilots whose endurance helped keep the island supplied and in Allied hands.

title: Words at War 43-09-02 (12) Dynamite Cargo (1943-09-02)
plotSynopsis: A dramatization of merchant seaman Fred Herman's Dynamite Cargo follows an Arctic convoy carrying wartime supplies toward Russia. Herman describes the strained, mixed crew aboard his cargo ship, repeated submarine and air attacks, and young Willie, whose dreams of returning to a girl in Galveston end when he is mortally wounded while helping defend the ship. After the vessel is lost, Herman and hundreds of other survivors crowd aboard the British cruiser Scylla and endure wave after wave of bombing, concluding that the merchant sailors keep returning to the run for reasons larger than pay alone.

title: Words at War 43-09-16 (14) Since You Went Away (1943-09-16)
plotSynopsis: Through letters to her absent husband, Anne Hilton describes how she and her daughters adjust after he leaves for military service. The family rents his room, takes on new responsibilities and tries to keep everyday life steady while fear, loneliness and wartime rumors strain them. A disturbing dinner conversation about servicemen abandoning families intensifies Anne's anxiety, but the episode ends when a long-awaited telephone call from London reaches her and confirms that her husband is safe.

title: Words at War 43-09-23 (15) They Shall Not Have Me (1943-09-23)
plotSynopsis: French prisoner John Hélion survives forced labor in Germany by clinging to one purpose: escape. Fellow prisoners pool maps, money, clothing, forged papers and hard-won knowledge from failed attempts, even disciplining a suspected informer to protect future plans. Hélion finally slips away in civilian disguise and travels through Germany by train, repeatedly risking exposure at inspections and among strangers. Near the border, sympathetic travelers help shield him, and he reaches freedom, dedicating his escape to the comrades whose collective effort made it possible.

title: Words at War 43-09-30 (16) Battle Hymn of China (1943-09-30)
plotSynopsis: A dramatized selection from Agnes Smedley's Battle Hymn of China presents episodes from her years among Chinese soldiers, guerrillas and civilians resisting Japan. She describes wounded men caring for one another, a dangerous night journey through enemy territory, life in guerrilla regions and her friendship with the young orderly Guo-wa, who joins the army partly for the chance to learn. Other scenes show villagers and fighters using patience, deception and local knowledge against occupying troops. The program is structured as eyewitness reportage and closes by presenting China's resistance as part of the wider Allied struggle.

title: Words at War 43-10-05 (17) Eighty-Three Days - the Survival of Seaman Izzi (1943-10-05)
sortKey: 0|1943-10-05|00017|words at war 43-10-05 (17) eighty-three days - the survival of seaman izzi (1943-10-05)
plotSynopsis: A dramatization of Mark Murphy's 83 Days recounts the true ordeal of Seaman Second Class Basil Izzi after his merchant ship is torpedoed in the South Atlantic. Izzi and a handful of survivors drift for nearly three months on rafts with dwindling food and water, watching companions weaken, go blind and die before being buried at sea. On the eighty-third day a U.S. patrol craft finally recognizes them as survivors and rescues the remaining men, ending one of the war's remarkable stories of endurance at sea.

title: Words at War 43-10-12 (18) Paris - Underground (1943-10-12)
plotSynopsis: American widow Etta Shiber and her friend Kitty turn their occupied Paris home into part of an escape network for stranded British soldiers. With forged papers, hospital contacts and help along the demarcation line, they move men toward unoccupied France until betrayal brings arrests. Several members of the network receive prison or death sentences, including Kitty, while Etta is sentenced to hard labor. She is later released in a prisoner exchange for a German spy and closes by honoring Kitty and the resistance work they carried on together.

title: Words at War 43-10-19 (19) Shortcut to Tokyo (1943-10-19)
plotSynopsis: Correspondent Corey Ford describes the largely unseen Aleutian campaign through the men fighting weather and Japanese forces in the fog-bound islands. Patrol crews discover enemy movements, bases are built under brutal conditions and pilots battle an environment that can be as deadly as combat. Ford becomes especially close to pilot Wally, who records a birthday message for his young son before later dying when his plane crashes in the fog. The account ends with new American bases pushing westward through the Aleutians, turning the islands into a possible shortcut toward Japan.

title: Words at War 43-10-26 (20) Who Dare to Live (1943-10-26)
plotSynopsis: Merchant captain Jack returns from wartime service physically recovered but shaken by the loss of a ship and crew, and fears that no company will trust him with another command. Given the freighter Sarah, he struggles through delays, crew trouble and a difficult Atlantic voyage while trying to prove he still belongs at sea. After reaching Halifax, he admits how much the ordeal has cost him. Told he needs rest rather than another command, Jack finally accepts that serving the merchant fleet in another capacity is still honorable service and agrees to go back to work.

title: Words at War 43-11-02 (21) Here Is Your War (1943-11-02)
plotSynopsis: A dramatized selection from Ernie Pyle's Here Is Your War presents his ground-level view of the North African campaign. Instead of following one plot, it moves through scenes of dirty camps, infantry marches, delayed letters from home, exhausted soldiers, combat deaths and brief moments of humor. Pyle emphasizes the ordinary men who carried the campaign and the gulf between their experience and life at home, ending with the North African fighting over and rows of white crosses left behind as the army prepares to move on to the next battlefield.

title: Words at War 43-11-09 (22) to All Hands (1943-11-09)
plotSynopsis: Lieutenant John Mason Brown dramatizes portions of his own To All Hands, recounting service aboard an American flagship during the amphibious invasion of Sicily. Assigned to the bridge, Brown broadcasts battle developments to sailors below decks who cannot see the action, describing the convoy, landings, air attacks and the anxious hours offshore. His farewell to the ship emphasizes the shared hardships and fellowship created by the campaign, comparing the crew's bond to Shakespeare's band of brothers after a common day of battle.

title: Words at War 43-11-23 (24) Escape from the Balkans (1943-11-23)
sortKey: 0|1943-11-23|00024|words at war 43-11-23 (24) escape from the balkans (1943-11-23)
plotSynopsis: Bulgarian journalist Michael Padev, a correspondent for British newspapers, is arrested after German influence tightens over wartime Bulgaria. Interrogation and torture give way to imprisonment in the Gondavoda camp, where he and fellow prisoners endure disease, deprivation and constant surveillance. Padev helps carry word of the camp to outside contacts and eventually joins an escape attempt using forged papers. After tense checks at the frontier, he reaches Turkey and freedom, while the broadcast links his story to the wider partisan struggle against fascist control of the Balkans.

title: Words at War 43-11-30 (25) Ave Duce - Sawdust Caesar - Balcony Empire (1943-11-30)
sortKey: 0|1943-11-30|00025|words at war 43-11-30 (25) ave duce - sawdust caesar - balcony empire (1943-11-30)
plotSynopsis: A satirical radio treatment of Mussolini and Italian fascism, based on Fruits of Fascism, Sawdust Caesar and Balcony Empire, lets the personified city of Rome address the fallen dictator directly. The program traces fascism's rise through intimidation, Blackshirt violence, the March on Rome, propaganda and the gradual destruction of elections, free speech and independent institutions. Rome mocks Mussolini's betrayals of the people, monarchy and church and ends by portraying Allied advance and Nazi occupation as signs that his promised empire has collapsed and a reckoning is approaching.

title: Words at War 43-12-07 (26) a Book of War Letters (1943-12-07)
plotSynopsis: A Pearl Harbor Day collection of dramatized letters written by servicemen from training camps and battlefronts. The letters move from hopes about citizenship, family and the future to firsthand accounts of combat, fear and exhaustion, including messages from Corregidor as surrender approaches. Rather than following one protagonist, the broadcast presents the war through many individual voices and closes with a final message from a trapped serviceman asking that his love be carried home to his family.

title: Words at War 43-12-14 (27) Mother America (1943-12-14)
plotSynopsis: A dramatization of Carlos P. Romulo's Mother America frames the fall of Bataan and Corregidor within a broader account of the American relationship with the Philippines. Romulo traces the islands from colonial rule through expanded schools, health programs, infrastructure, political participation and the Filipino demand for eventual independence, arguing that democratic guidance should lead toward self-government rather than permanent domination. He closes by presenting Philippine independence as a model for a postwar world in which freedom, education and fair treatment replace imperial rule.

title: Words at War 43-12-21 (28) Log Book - British Merchant Marine (1943-12-21)
sortKey: 0|1943-12-21|00028|words at war 43-12-21 (28) log book - british merchant marine (1943-12-21)
plotSynopsis: A dramatization of Frank Laskier's Log Book follows a troubled young Englishman from reformatory life into the British Merchant Marine. Harsh ships, poverty and rough treatment nearly deepen his alienation, but fellowship at sea and wartime service give him a renewed sense of purpose. After his ship is torpedoed and he loses a leg, the sailor reflects on the social failures that shaped men like him while insisting that merchant seamen will help win the war and should also have a voice in building a better peace afterward.

title: Words at War 43-12-28 (29) Ninth Commandment - Invasion of Holland (1943-12-28)
sortKey: 0|1943-12-28|00029|words at war 43-12-28 (29) ninth commandment - invasion of holland (1943-12-28)
plotSynopsis: A dramatization of Hendrik Willem van Loon's The Ninth Commandment follows Samuel, a devout Dutch picture-frame maker who takes in a German refugee boy before the war. Samuel punishes the child for lying, creating a grievance that resurfaces years later when the grown boy returns under Nazi occupation. Given a chance to save his own life by signing a false statement denying the old incident, Samuel refuses to bear false witness even against himself and is executed rather than violate the commandment he once taught the boy.

title: Words at War 44-01-04 (30) They Shall Inherit the Earth (1944-01-04)
sortKey: 0|1944-01-04|00030|words at war 44-01-04 (30) they shall inherit the earth (1944-01-04)
plotSynopsis: A dramatization based on Otto Zoff's They Shall Inherit the Earth examines what modern war has done to children in different countries. Scenes contrast ordinary childhood play with militarization, hunger, displacement, bombing and the emotional damage suffered by children in Europe and elsewhere. The program ends with a promise that the adults who survive must feed, find and protect the young, while teaching them enough trust in other people to inherit a world less governed by fear and war.

title: Words at War 44-01-11 (31) Eighty-Three Days - the Survival of Seaman Izzi (1944-01-11)
sortKey: 0|1944-01-11|00031|words at war 44-01-11 (31) eighty-three days - the survival of seaman izzi (1944-01-11)
plotSynopsis: After a torpedo sinks his ship in the South Atlantic, Seaman Basil Izzi and a handful of survivors crowd onto a raft with almost no food or water. Over eighty-three days they endure hunger, thirst, storms, injuries, deaths and the repeated heartbreak of aircraft and ships passing without seeing them. As the men weaken, Izzi watches companions die and struggles to remain conscious himself. On the eighty-third day, an American patrol craft finally spots the raft and rescues the survivors, who are carried aboard and slowly nursed back to health.

title: Words at War 44-01-18 (32) War Tide (1944-01-18)
plotSynopsis: A dramatization of Lin Tai Yi's War Tide follows young Loyin as war destroys the ordinary life of her Chinese family. Her brother goes to fly against the Japanese, her father dies after setting fire to his shop, and Loyin helps lead her mother, grandmother, sister-in-law and little brother through invasion, violence and flight; her grandmother even uses her nine-fingered hand to frighten away a threatening soldier by claiming leprosy. Reunited with the wounded Shen, Loyin accepts his proposal and the story closes on the idea of the war tide as the anger, courage and endurance that keeps people moving forward despite continuing danger.

title: Condition Red (1944-01-25)
plotSynopsis: A documentary-style adaptation of Captain Frederick J. Bell's Condition Red uses the destroyer he calls the G to explain life and combat aboard a U.S. Navy destroyer in the South Pacific. It moves from a Japanese air attack to damage control, anti-submarine tactics, the responsibilities expected of junior officers, cramped living conditions and the ship's constant readiness for another alarm. Rather than one continuous plot, the broadcast combines action scenes with Bell's descriptions of destroyer crews, training, endurance and the peculiar pride sailors develop in an uncomfortable but hard-hitting ship.

title: The White Brigade (1944-02-01)
plotSynopsis: Belgian civilian Jean Boucher joins the White Brigade resistance after the German occupation and takes part in espionage, sabotage and escape work while his family lives under constant threat. The Gestapo closes in, Jean is eventually killed while trying to escape, and his wife Denise loses their child after the Germans take her away. When the occupiers threaten to execute one hundred hostages unless the killer of a German officer confesses, Denise falsely claims responsibility so the hostages will be freed. Facing death herself, she tells a priest that sacrifice has become part of the resistance oath she and Jean accepted.

title: George Washington Carver (1944-02-08)
plotSynopsis: A biographical dramatization traces George Washington Carver from a child born into slavery to the scientist and teacher who transformed agricultural research at Tuskegee Institute. Carver pursues education despite poverty and racism, then accepts Booker T. Washington's invitation to Alabama, where he builds a laboratory from discarded materials and attacks the South's dependence on cotton. His experiments with crops such as peanuts and sweet potatoes create new uses for depleted land and help poor farmers diversify. Framed as a tribute on Abraham Lincoln's birthday, the program presents Carver's life as proof that talent and service are not determined by race.

title: The New Sun (1944-02-15)
plotSynopsis: A dramatization of Japanese artist Taro Yashima's The New Sun recounts his opposition to militarism and fascism inside prewar Japan. His drawings criticize military domination, leading to arrest, interrogation and brutal treatment alongside other political prisoners, while his pregnant wife and comrades also suffer under repression. Persuaded to sign a false confession so he can leave prison and continue the struggle through his art, Yashima eventually reaches the United States and uses his freedom to describe the Japanese anti-fascist resistance and expose the system he escaped.

title: Assignment Usa (1944-02-22)
plotSynopsis: A documentary-style adaptation of Selden Menefee's Assignment USA surveys wartime America after a 15,000-mile reporting trip. The program praises enormous industrial and military effort while also confronting racial discrimination, southern economic grievances, labor-management conflict, housing shortages and other weaknesses that divide the home front. Menefee appears at the end to affirm that Americans are broadly committed to democratic war aims and argues that informed citizens must correct those failures if the country is to win both the war and the peace.

title: The Weeping Wood (1944-03-07)
plotSynopsis: A dramatic impression of Vicki Baum's The Weeping Wood tells the global story of natural rubber through exploitation, plantation development, war and scientific innovation. Scenes move from abused Amazon rubber gatherers and the removal of rubber seeds to British-controlled plantations, to the loss of Asian supplies after Japanese conquest and the wartime drive for synthetic rubber and renewed production in the Americas. The program presents rubber as both a source of wealth and suffering while ending on the hope that technology and better labor conditions can break that cycle.

title: Science at War (1944-03-14)
plotSynopsis: A documentary-style adaptation of George W. Gray's Science at War asks whether scientific progress is responsible for modern destruction or merely a tool shaped by human choices. Through dramatized examples involving poison gas, magnetic mines, mine detectors, battlefield medicine and wartime engineering, it shows science creating weapons and also countering them or saving lives. The program concludes that knowledge cannot simply be reversed and that humanity must decide whether scientific power will serve war or a shared peaceful future.

title: Der Fuehrer (1944-03-21)
plotSynopsis: A dramatization based on Conrad Heiden's Der Fuehrer traces the fabrication and political use of the anti-Semitic Protocols of the Elders of Zion. The program follows the forged document from Russian secret-police manipulation through pogrom propaganda and into Nazi ideology, showing how false conspiracy claims were repurposed to divide populations, justify persecution and offer a political blueprint to Hitler and his followers. It closes by identifying the forgery as a deliberate lie whose spread helped prepare the ground for mass violence against Jews and other minorities.

title: A Bell for Adano (1944-03-28)
plotSynopsis: A dramatization of John Hersey's A Bell for Adano follows Italian-American Major Victor Joppolo as he administers the newly occupied town of Adano. He works to restore food, water, local government and the carts residents need for daily life, while also pursuing a replacement for the town bell taken away under fascism. Joppolo defies General Marvin's blanket ban on carts because he believes it harms the people and is eventually relieved for disobeying the order, but as he leaves Adano he hears the new bell ringing over the town he tried to serve.

title: Wild River (1944-04-11)
plotSynopsis: A radio impression of Anna Louise Strong's Wild River traces the building of the great Dnieper dam as a symbol of Soviet industrialization and collective sacrifice. Workers endure primitive housing, shortages and years of difficult labor to tame the river, generate power and transform the region. When the German invasion threatens to seize the project, the same people who built it choose to destroy the dam rather than surrender it, promising that they will return after victory and build again.

title: The Silence of the Sea (1944-04-18)
plotSynopsis: A dramatization of Vercors' The Silence of the Sea follows an elderly Frenchman and his niece after a cultured German officer is billeted in their occupied home. They answer his nightly monologues with deliberate silence while he speaks hopefully of a future reconciliation between Germany and France. After a visit to Paris reveals that Nazi policy aims to destroy French culture rather than unite with it, the disillusioned officer asks for transfer to combat; the niece finally breaks her silence to say goodbye as he leaves.

title: The Curtain Rises (1944-05-02)
plotSynopsis: A dramatization of Quentin Reynolds' The Curtain Rises follows the correspondent from another departure overseas through Allied campaigns in Russia, North Africa, Sicily and Italy. Reynolds is especially struck by American soldiers in their first major combat, describing both their toughness and their restraint toward civilians and prisoners. After witnessing the costly fighting in Sicily and at Salerno, he returns home warning Americans against complacency: the campaigns so far were only the prelude, and the difficult invasion of German-held Europe still lies ahead.

title: Gunners Get Glory (1944-05-09)
plotSynopsis: Navy armed-guard officer Bob Berry recalls being rushed through wartime training and sent to defend merchant ships against submarine and air attack. His service includes the sinking of a ship, hours in an oil-covered sea and survival in a lifeboat with other crewmen while they ration food, water and cigarettes. Berry eventually returns home, physically safe but marked by what happened at sea. When friends invite him and his wife to a swimming party, the idea is unbearable, and the story closes with the couple awaiting the birth of their child.

title: Lifeline (1944-05-16)
plotSynopsis: A dramatization of Robert Carse's Lifeline honors the United States Merchant Marine and the dangerous supply routes that sustained Allied forces. An able seaman describes Arctic convoys, sinkings, lifeboat ordeals and the poor treatment merchant crews sometimes received ashore, then recounts the courage of shipmates carrying men and supplies into combat zones. The closing Guadalcanal episode follows a merchant sailor who volunteers to handle landing craft under fire, is badly wounded getting Marines ashore and dies after completing his job.

title: Lend Lease-Weapon for Victory (1944-05-23)
plotSynopsis: A documentary-style dramatization of Edward Stettinius Jr.'s Lend-Lease: Weapon for Victory explains the program through analogies, historical narration and scenes from Allied fronts. It traces the shift from American hesitation to becoming the 'arsenal of democracy,' then depicts tanks, food, aircraft and other supplies reaching Britain and other Allies while reverse lend-lease also supports American forces overseas. Stettinius appears at the end to argue that pooling production, resources and military strength among the United Nations was essential to stopping Axis expansion and winning the war.

title: The Navy Hunts the Cgr 3070 (1944-05-30)
plotSynopsis: The Coast Guard Reserve yacht CGR-3070 begins an ordinary coastal picket patrol searching for enemy submarines, but a severe Atlantic storm turns the mission into a survival ordeal. The small craft is battered, flooded and damaged, several men are injured, and a tow from a British destroyer later parts in heavy weather. With the radio failing and rescue attempts repeatedly missing them, the crew patches the boat, rations what remains and keeps sailing. A convoy is unable to take them off, but the men refuse to give up, and a patrol vessel finally finds them off the North Carolina coast. Every crewman walks ashore, embarrassed only that they never actually sighted a German submarine.

title: Xx War Bond Special (1944-06-13)
plotSynopsis: A War Bond special reprises dramatized passages from Ernie Pyle's Here's Your War about American infantrymen in North Africa. Pyle describes exhausted soldiers carrying heavy weapons after days of combat, their longing for home, their kindness toward local children and the emotional changes produced by prolonged fighting. The program ends among the graves of men left behind as units move to the next battlefield, using Pyle's account to urge listeners to support the surviving soldiers through the purchase of war bonds.

title: Fair Stood the Wind for France (1944-06-27)
plotSynopsis: A wounded British airman crash-lands in occupied France and is hidden by a French family while recovering from severe injuries that eventually cost him an arm. As German pressure closes in, he forms a deep bond with the young woman Francoise and is helped by his surviving comrades and French allies. The fugitives make a dangerous journey toward Spain, repeatedly risking discovery. Near the border, O'Connor sacrifices himself to distract the authorities after Francoise is detained, allowing the airman and Francoise to escape the final stretch toward freedom together.

title: War Criminals and Punishment (1944-07-04)
plotSynopsis: A policy-driven dramatization of George Creel's War Criminals and Punishment argues that Axis leaders must not escape accountability after the war. Using historical examples from the aftermath of World War I, staged voices outline ways German leaders previously avoided punishment and warn against repeating those failures. The program calls for unconditional surrender, military occupation and disarmament, prosecution of war criminals and the destruction of Prussian militarism as necessary steps toward a durable peace.

title: Captain Retread (1944-07-11)
plotSynopsis: A humorous autobiographical adaptation of Donald Hough's Captain Retread follows a middle-aged World War I veteran returning to uniform as an Air Force captain. Through loosely connected vignettes, Hough buys an over-tight uniform he expects to slim into, adjusts to training and Army routines, reflects on the humor and strain of military life, and compares experiences with his Marine son Sherwood. The program closes with father and son playfully awarding Hough's wife Barry a family 'citation' for enduring their service, mixing comedy with reflections on the sacrifices surrounding wartime service.

title: War Below Zero (1944-07-18)
plotSynopsis: A dramatization of War Below Zero follows American servicemen assigned to isolated weather stations on Greenland's ice cap. Their enemy is primarily cold, blizzards, loneliness and the strain of maintaining weather reports despite months without confirmation that their transmissions are being received. The men continue their work, assist after a bomber crashes in their remote area and eventually learn that their reports did reach command and helped support Allied operations, earning praise before they rotate home for rest.

title: Lost Island (1944-07-25)
plotSynopsis: Army engineer Major George Dodd arrives on a peaceful South Pacific island to prepare it for conversion into an American airbase. As he grows close to Ruth, Vigo, Father Vincent and the island community, he realizes the runways and military facilities will erase homes, gardens, sacred meeting places and even Vigo's turtle nesting ground. The islanders initially welcome the arriving ship because they do not understand what it means. Dodd is devastated by the destruction but accepts the base as part of defeating fascism, and he and Ruth remain to help the displaced people endure the loss while the new airfield rises.

title: Headquarters Budapest (1944-08-01)
plotSynopsis: A dramatization based on Robert Parker's Headquarters Budapest uses satire and reported scenes to examine corruption, dictatorship and political weakness in the prewar Balkans. The program portrays rulers such as Prince Paul, King Carol and other regional leaders as divided from their own people while Hitler exploits economic dependence, territorial rivalries and authoritarian politics to extend German influence. Parker closes by warning that another world war could again begin in the Balkans unless the region receives education, economic opportunity, democratic government and a coherent postwar policy from the major Allied powers.

title: Nazis Go Underground (1944-08-08)
plotSynopsis: A warning-oriented dramatization argues that Nazi power could survive military defeat by moving underground. Staged scenes show German officials planning infiltration, propaganda, sabotage and the placement of loyal personnel inside institutions likely to be used by occupying forces. The broadcast broadens the warning beyond Germany, arguing that fascism thrives wherever fear, racial hatred, poverty and political manipulation are allowed to grow, and concludes that military victory must be followed by dismantling Nazi organization and improving the conditions that make fascism attractive.

title: Heaven Below-China Looks Forwardfirst Half (1944-08-15)
plotSynopsis: This staged first-half recording combines material from E. H. Clayton's Heaven Below and Sun Fo's China Looks Forward to examine wartime China. Through missionary observations and dramatized examples, it contrasts village superstition, poverty and limited education with the endurance of ordinary Chinese people resisting Japanese invasion. The excerpt then turns inward, with Sun Fo sharply criticizing Chinese political leadership, mass ignorance and authoritarian habits inside the Nationalist system. The surviving staged audio ends during that critique, so no later portion of the original broadcast is inferred.

title: Simone (1944-08-29)
plotSynopsis: Fifteen-year-old Simone lives with her prosperous uncle as France collapses before the German advance. She discovers that he has hoarded gasoline, profiteered from refugees and intends to preserve his garage and vehicles for the occupiers rather than destroy them. Inspired by the example of Joan of Arc and by Maurice's warnings about collaboration, Simone steals the garage key and burns the entire property so the Germans cannot use it. Her uncle and local collaborators then try to force her to sign a false nonpolitical confession, but she refuses and is sent away still openly defiant.

title: The Veteran Comes Back (1944-09-05)
plotSynopsis: A dramatized discussion of Willard Waller's The Veteran Comes Back examines the political and social danger created when returning servicemen are denied work, security and respect. Historical scenes from earlier American wars, including the Bonus Expeditionary Force of 1932, are used to show how neglected veterans can become bitter and vulnerable to demagogues. A contemporary G.I. voice closes by demanding jobs, housing, education, medical care and social security so millions of returning veterans can help build a better country instead of being driven against it.

title: One Man Air Force (1944-09-12)
plotSynopsis: A dramatization of the wartime career of fighter pilot Don Gentile traces his fascination with flying from reckless youthful aviation in Ohio to combat service against Germany. Once war comes, the instincts that worried his family become disciplined skill in the air, where he earns a reputation as an exceptional fighter ace while remaining personally shy and self-effacing. The broadcast closes with Gentile's mother speaking in person, saying that she came to understand why her son and other American servicemen had to fight to protect their homes.

title: The Time for Decision-U.s.War Aims (1944-09-19)
plotSynopsis: A policy-focused dramatization drawing on Sumner Welles's The Time for Decision and Walter Lippmann's U.S. War Aims asks what kind of peace can prevent another world war. Through family scenes, historical comparisons and direct argument, it warns that military victory alone will fail if nations return to isolation, power politics and unresolved rivalries. The broadcast urges Americans to study competing plans for international security and decide whether the next generation will inherit a durable peace or an even more destructive war.

title: Journey Through Chaos (1944-09-26)
plotSynopsis: A dramatized survey of American social problems argues that the nation cannot win a war for freedom abroad while ignoring fear and division at home. Scenes examine slum housing, juvenile delinquency, racial discrimination in both North and South, and labor-management conflict. The recurring diagnosis is fear: fear of neighbors, workers, minorities and social change. The program closes by arguing that teamwork, reason and individual responsibility are needed to confront these problems rather than hiding them.

title: Pacific Victory 1945 (1944-10-03)
plotSynopsis: A dramatized adaptation of correspondent Joseph Driscoll's Pacific Victory 1945 surveys the American war against Japan and argues that victory depends on men, leadership, weapons and sustained support from the home front. It profiles commanders including MacArthur, Nimitz and Halsey, recalls the cost paid by wounded and dead servicemen, and rejects the idea of an easy shortcut to defeating Japan. The broadcast ends by urging civilians not to relax as the European war advances and to treat victory in the Pacific as an urgent national goal.

title: The Veteran Comes Back (1944-10-10)
plotSynopsis: A documentary-style dramatization of Willard Waller's The Veteran Comes Back examines the social problems awaiting American servicemen returning from war. Through staged testimony from veterans of earlier conflicts, scenes of unemployment and crime, and the voice of a contemporary G.I., the program argues that neglect, bitterness and economic insecurity can make returning veterans a danger to themselves and society. It closes with a call for jobs, housing, education, medical care and social security rather than empty praise or bonuses alone.

title: Still Time to Die (1944-10-24)
plotSynopsis: A dramatization of correspondent Jack Belden's Still Time to Die rejects sanitized or triumphalist descriptions of modern war. Recovering from wounds, Belden recalls the hunger, bombing, fear and misery he witnessed from Malta to the battlefields of Europe and contrasts those realities with confident commentary heard far from combat. Returning to the United States, he warns that prejudice, reaction and authoritarian thinking can exist at home as well as abroad, and concludes that military victory must be joined to a continuing fight for genuine democratic freedom.

title: One Damn Thing After Another (1944-11-14)
plotSynopsis: A dramatization of correspondent Tom Treanor's One Damn Thing After Another recounts his comic and dangerous path from low-priority, often unauthorized war reporter to an accepted front-line correspondent. Treanor talks his way toward the fighting, borrows transportation, joins a bombing mission against orders, is repeatedly reprimanded or expelled from theaters of operation, and keeps mailing full newspaper stories when other correspondents cable theirs. The broadcast then steps outside the book to note that Treanor later covered Normandy for the Los Angeles Times and NBC and was killed in action, ending with a roll of newspaper and radio correspondents who had died covering the war.

title: Barriers Down (1944-11-21)
plotSynopsis: A documentary-style adaptation of Kent Cooper's Barriers Down argues that monopolies and national controls over international news helped create prejudice and war. Dramatized examples show how distorted reporting encouraged nations to distrust one another, while the program traces Cooper's campaign for independent news exchange. Cooper appears in person at the end to call for a peace settlement guaranteeing worldwide freedom of the press, equal access to official information and communications, and protection against propaganda disguised as news.

title: Camp Follower (1944-11-28)
plotSynopsis: Army wife Barbara follows her husband from post to post, learning how difficult wartime life can be for women trying to stay near soldiers whose orders change without warning. She encounters crowded housing, shortages, dismissive officials and repeated disappointments, but also friendships with other Army wives facing the same uncertainty. Just after her husband finally receives permission to live off post, the order is canceled because his unit is shipping out. Barbara packs again and follows to the next camp, recognizing that she has become a true camp follower through loyalty rather than convenience.

title: The Guys on the Ground (1944-12-05)
plotSynopsis: A framed collection of dramatized accounts from Alfred Friendly's The Guys on the Ground honors the Air Force service crews who keep combat aircraft operating. Three pilots relaxing after a bond rally tell a reporter about mechanics, engineers and other ground personnel building runways, repairing damaged planes under fire and working for days without rest. The program emphasizes that celebrated air victories depend on largely anonymous crews whose motto is that the difficult is done immediately and the impossible merely takes longer.

title: Your School Your Children (1944-12-12)
plotSynopsis: A dramatization of Marie Syrkin's Your School, Your Children argues that public schools must directly confront racial, religious and political prejudice rather than avoiding controversial subjects. Classroom and faculty scenes show antisemitism, anti-Black bias and administrative reluctance to challenge intolerance, while Syrkin worries that students can carry those attitudes into adult life. The broadcast points to the Springfield Plan as a working model that teaches democratic self-government, evidence-based judgment and respect for every individual as part of the regular curriculum.

title: The Cross and the Arrow (1944-12-19)
plotSynopsis: German tank-factory worker Willie Wegler becomes disgusted by forced labor, militarism and his own part in feeding the Nazi war machine. He arranges hay in the shape of an arrow and sets it alight to guide British bombers toward the hidden factory, but is shot and drawn into a Gestapo investigation. The authorities conceal the truth and blame a Polish forced laborer to protect factory morale. Wegler survives long enough to see the bombers return, satisfied that his signal was seen and hoping his act of refusal will inspire others.

title: Scapegoats in History-History of Bigotry in the United States (1944-12-26)
sortKey: 0|1944-12-26|00071|scapegoats in history-history of bigotry in the united states (1944-12-26)
plotSynopsis: A Christmas-season dramatization based on Kenneth Gould's Scapegoats in History and Gustavus Myers' History of Bigotry in the United States surveys the recurring use of persecuted groups as targets for fear and social blame. Beginning with Herod and moving through witch trials, anti-Catholicism, anti-Irish prejudice, antisemitism and discrimination against other minorities, the program argues that fabricated accusations allow societies to redirect economic and political frustrations toward innocent people. It closes by rejecting scapegoating as contrary to both democratic justice and the religious ideals associated with Christmas.

title: Its Always Tomorrow (1945-01-02)
plotSynopsis: American reporter Dave Sedgwick is sent to wartime England, where he meets Polly, a working-class waitress who distrusts patriotic slogans and the privileged people she serves. As Dave reports on factory workers, rationing, taxes and soldiers, he comes to see that many Britons are fighting not for empire but for a fairer postwar society. Dave and Polly fall in love, but she still refuses to romanticize the war. After a bombing badly wounds Dave, Polly agrees to leave her restaurant job for war work because she loves him, while insisting they must also fight to make sure ordinary people are not cheated after victory.

title: Borrowed Night (1945-01-09)
plotSynopsis: A dramatization of Oscar Ray's Borrowed Night follows an Alsatian forced into the German army who attempts to escape service by feigning traumatic neurosis. In a military hospital he watches German doctors expose other suspected malingerers and send them to execution, while his own deception becomes increasingly dangerous. After a fellow patient kills the doctor examining him, he escapes the hospital and crosses Germany, ending with his determination to regain his strength, join the French forces and return against the system he fled.

title: Verdict on India (1945-01-16)
plotSynopsis: A radio treatment of Beverly Nichols' Verdict on India examines British rule and the political and social problems facing India near the end of the war. Nichols discusses public health, poverty, caste, purdah, the joint-family system, British social isolation and the lack of Indian control over military and industrial resources, while arguing that continued imperial rule cannot be morally justified. The program concludes that Britain should leave, but stresses that independence also requires Indians themselves to confront internal divisions and build the institutions needed for self-government and defense.

title: Story of a Secret State (1945-01-23)
plotSynopsis: Polish officer Jan Karski recounts how the German invasion destroys his prewar life and draws him into the Polish underground. He describes the clandestine courts, sabotage, forged documents, financing and resistance networks that keep an underground state functioning under occupation. Karski is eventually smuggled into the Warsaw ghetto, where he witnesses starvation, terror and random killing. He escapes Poland carrying evidence of Nazi crimes and resolves to report to the outside world what the underground and the persecuted population are enduring.

title: Ten Escape from Tojosecond Half (1945-02-06)
plotSynopsis: This second-half recording presents dramatic excerpts from Lieutenant William Kelly's Ten Escape from Tojo centered on Allied prisoners in Japanese camps in the Philippines. Former prisoners describe starvation, disease, executions, the Bataan Death March and the refusal of guards to provide even basic care or burial for the dead, while the narration connects these accounts to the recent rescue of 513 prisoners from Cabanatuan. The program closes by insisting that the testimony be remembered as evidence of how American and Filipino prisoners were treated during the occupation.

title: What to Do with Germany (1945-02-13)
plotSynopsis: An argumentative dramatization of Louis Nizer's What to Do with Germany frames its policy case inside a fictional 1985 America enslaved by a resurgent Germany. A father explains how the postwar Allies failed to disarm German militarism, then the program surveys earlier German leaders, nationalist doctrine, Nazi education and the weakness of relying on an imagined democratic underground. The broadcast advocates military, economic and ideological disarmament and warns that failing to reform German institutions could allow another world war and the destruction of democratic freedom.

title: Battle Report-Pearl Harbor to the Coral Sea (1945-02-20)
sortKey: 0|1945-02-20|00070|battle report-pearl harbor to the coral sea (1945-02-20)
plotSynopsis: A dramatization from Battle Report personifies the submarine tender USS Canopus as she recounts her role in the doomed defense of Bataan and Corregidor. Damaged but still operating, the ship is disguised to appear destroyed while her repair facilities support the fighting, and members of her crew later serve ashore as improvised infantry. When Bataan falls, the crew takes Canopus into deep water and scuttles her rather than surrender the ship, while the closing narration promises that the Navy will preserve her name in a new vessel.

title: Faith of Our Fighters-The Bid Was Four Hearts (1945-02-27)
sortKey: 0|1945-02-27|00003|faith of our fighters-the bid was four hearts (1945-02-27)
plotSynopsis: A dramatization of the final voyage of the troop transport Dorchester follows Army chaplains George Fox, Alexander Goode, Clark Poling and John Washington as they minister to soldiers of different faiths aboard ship. When the Dorchester is torpedoed near Greenland, panic spreads as men struggle for lifeboats and life jackets. The four chaplains help others to safety and each gives his own life jacket to a soldier who has none. Witnesses later remember seeing the chaplains praying together on the slanting deck as the ship sinks beneath them.

title: The Rainbow (1945-03-06)
plotSynopsis: A dramatization of Wanda Wasilewska's The Rainbow depicts a Ukrainian village under Nazi occupation and the resistance growing around it. Partisan Olena Kostyuk returns while pregnant, is arrested and tortured rather than reveal guerrilla positions, while villagers resist German grain demands and secretly pass military information to the partisans. After the Germans order Olena and her newborn killed, the guerrillas attack the village; the closing image of a rainbow over the fighting is presented as a sign of hope beyond the occupation.

title: Can Do (1945-03-13)
plotSynopsis: A dramatized adaptation of William Bradford Huie's Can Do surveys the wartime work of the Navy Seabees through a veteran narrator looking back after discharge. The program moves through construction under fire, beach landings, mines, airstrips and the deaths of fellow workers rather than following one continuous plot. It emphasizes the Seabees' mixture of engineering and combat, including a doctor's decision to save a wounded Japanese prisoner, and closes with the narrator describing the Seabees' pride in building whatever the Navy needs wherever the war takes them.

title: Tomorrow Will Sing (1945-03-20)
plotSynopsis: A dramatization of Elliott Arnold's Tomorrow Will Sing follows Italian-American airman Eddie Amato as he helps villagers near his wartime base understand American democratic ideas. The farmers come to trust Eddie while confronting old fascist influence and unfair economic practices, but he is later court-martialed after being accused of robbing local peasants. Testimony finally exposes a former Blackshirt's son as the real thief, clearing Eddie; the story closes with Eddie sent on to the Pacific and remembered in the village as proof that democracy can be expressed through ordinary decency.

title: Banshee Harvest (1945-03-27)
plotSynopsis: Captain Arthur Curtin returns to the Irish countryside of his childhood and becomes entangled in a bitter struggle between impoverished tenant farmers, powerful ranching interests and political forces exploiting wartime Ireland. What begins as a visit to his uncle grows into a conflict over land, labor and dignity as Curtin sees how deeply the local poor are trapped. An attempted revolt is crushed, its leaders killed or hanged, and the survivors return to hardship. Curtin escapes because of his family connection, left to question whether the failed struggle nevertheless proved that ordinary people were right to fight for freedom and a decent life.

title: Full Employment in a Free Society (1945-04-03)
plotSynopsis: A policy dramatization of William Beveridge's Full Employment in a Free Society frames the postwar economy as a fork in the road between Depression and Full Employment. A returning veteran is shown the human cost of mass unemployment, then guided through Beveridge's argument that government should sustain demand, protect citizens from unemployment and support social security, health care, education and decent housing. Critics challenge the plan as excessive state control, while the broadcast answers that full employment is meant to remove fear and insecurity without abolishing individual freedom.

title: Apartment in Athens (1945-04-10)
plotSynopsis: In occupied Athens, Nicholas Helianos deliberately takes a German officer, Captain Kalter, into his family home in hopes that apparent cooperation will protect them. The arrangement humiliates his wife Zoe and son Alex, while Kalter dominates the household and the family learns how dangerous even small acts of resistance can be. After a trip home, Kalter returns shattered by the deaths of his wife and son. Nicholas briefly sympathizes with him, then condemns the leaders who caused both Greek and German suffering. Kalter responds by summoning the military police. Facing execution, Nicholas sends Alex to join relatives in the mountains and leaves him one final lesson: never trust the occupier.

title: They Left the Back Door Open (1945-04-17)
plotSynopsis: John Donaldson recounts the life of his brother Bill, a working-class Canadian whose belief in British ideals collapses when he sees injustice and indifference toward fascism. Bill deserts the British Army, goes to Spain to fight with the International Brigades and earns the loyalty of the people around him through courage and good humor. During the Republican collapse, he volunteers for a diversionary attack so others can escape. Armed only with a club and a few grenades among his men, Bill is last seen charging a machine-gun position and dies helping open the way to safety.

title: Brave Men (1945-04-24)
plotSynopsis: A tribute to Ernie Pyle built from dramatized passages of Brave Men rather than one continuous story. The program moves among infantrymen waiting for battle, battlefield deaths, exhausted troops, small moments of tenderness and Pyle's observations about the bond among men living constantly with death. It repeatedly contrasts the reality of casualties with the simplified picture of victory at home, then closes by recalling Pyle's own death on Ie Shima and the soldiers who buried him as one of their own.

title: The Hide Out (1945-05-01)
plotSynopsis: A dramatization of Egon Hostovsky's The Hideout follows a Czech engineer living secretly in a cellar after fleeing Nazi persecution and becoming cut off from his wife and former life. His long isolation turns inward until a chance encounter with an old German acquaintance and contact with resistance members force him to confront the selfishness and fear behind his hiding. When the underground asks him to use his engineering knowledge for sabotage, he finally agrees, choosing to risk death and become part of the resistance instead of remaining trapped by fear.

title: The Road to Serfdom (1945-05-15)
plotSynopsis: A radio discussion of Friedrich Hayek's The Road to Serfdom presents his warning that centralized peacetime economic planning can concentrate power and erode individual liberty. Through staged arguments about business rules, job choice, competition, government authority and wartime regimentation, Hayek distinguishes temporary controls accepted for war from permanent controls adopted for security. He also rejects monopoly and special privilege as distortions of free enterprise. The program closes by arguing that political and economic freedom both require vigilance and that competition should be made fairer rather than replaced by central direction.

title: Wartime Racketeers (1945-05-22)
plotSynopsis: A warning about home-front crime dramatizes the many ways racketeers exploit wartime shortages, regulations and grief. Episodes cover scalped train tickets, black-market food and gasoline, counterfeit ration coupons, fraudulent allotment marriages and impostors who demand money from families of servicemen. The broadcast argues that these schemes survive because ordinary citizens cooperate with them and urges the public to report fraud, obey rationing rules and deny criminals the customers they need.

title: Soldier to Civilian (1945-05-29)
plotSynopsis: Using George K. Pratt's Soldier to Civilian as its guide, this dramatization follows returning veteran Ross as he discovers that coming home does not instantly restore the life he imagined overseas. His family treats him as fragile, his relationship with Christine strains under changed expectations, and difficulties finding satisfying work leave him frustrated and isolated. At a town meeting, Ross explains that veterans need useful jobs, independence, patience and ordinary common sense more than pity, parades or permanent hero treatment, framing readjustment as a problem civilians and veterans must solve together.

title: My Country-A Poem of America (1945-06-05)
plotSynopsis: Russell Davenport adapts his own My Country: A Poem of America into a patriotic radio meditation on the nation's people, work, homes, history and democratic inheritance. Multiple voices celebrate farmers, builders, families and servicemen while also treating freedom as an obligation passed from earlier generations through those dying in the current war. The poem closes by arguing that American liberty cannot remain private or isolated: freedom must be shared so that the democratic promise defended at home can extend to people beyond America's borders.

title: Words at War Intro
